entry.title: Speculative decoding lands on Metal - Qwen 3.8's NextN head and Gemma 4's assistant drafter.
entry.content: Both drafter families that ship with their models now run on any Apple GPU dasLLAMA runs on, and the depth is a per-box knob the tuner mints. Measured against a stock llama.cpp on identical rendered prompts: gemma-4-26B-A4B on an M5 Max goes 122.7 to 145.9 tok/s at depth 1 (llama.cpp 97.7 to 133.7), Qwen3.8-27B on an M4 Pro 12.7 to 14.0 (llama.cpp 11.5 to 13.8). How we measured, what we tried, and why the gain is as small as it is: the story.

entry.title: Speculative decoding on a Mac - what we tried, how we measured it, and how small the gain is.
entry.content:
Speculative decoding is the trick where a small drafter guesses the next few tokens and the big model checks all of them in one pass. If the guesses are good, you get several tokens for the price of a little more than one step. Two current model families ship their own drafter: Qwen 3.8 carries a NextN head - one extra transformer layer that predicts the token after next - and Gemma 4 ships a four-layer assistant model beside the 26B trunk. Both are now supported on Metal, on any Apple GPU dasLLAMA runs on. This is the story of getting there and of measuring what it is worth.

What we tried

Depth. A round drafts k tokens and verifies k + 1 rows. Depth 1 is the safe bet; depth 2 pays off only when the second guess is right often enough to cover a third verify row. We raced depth 1 against depth 2 on each box and made the answer a box knob the tuner mints (mtp_depth_nextn, mtp_depth_assistant). Every box we own minted 1. Depth 3 and 4 lost outright on the development rail and never reached the ruler.

Width. Verifying the top-2 or top-3 candidates at one position instead of a chain. We dropped it on paper: with one token ahead there is no room for a second candidate to win, and combined with depth it multiplies the verify rows the round cannot afford.

A depth controller. An online controller that raises depth while acceptance stays high. Dropped in favour of the box knob; it may return as per-request depth, because acceptance is a property of the prompt, not the box - the math prompt below runs 94% at position 1.

The drafter's input. The Gemma drafter takes the trunk's hidden state as input. Pre-norm lost to post-norm on acceptance; post-norm ships. The target's quantization is not what caps acceptance: the Q8_0 Gemma target accepted 76.5% against the Q4_K_M target's 74.6% on the same corpus.

The kernels. Verify rows on K-quant weights ride a small-batch GEMV that streams each weight row once for all rows. That kernel is ALU-bound, and Apple GPUs differ in how much ALU they have per byte of bandwidth. The M5 Max likes one form; the M4 Pro needed a different one - a register tile where each thread owns two weight rows and both activation columns - and, above two rows, a walk of that tile over column pairs instead of the four-column kernel. Which form a box gets is decided by a race at tune time and stored in its sidecar, like every other kernel choice in the engine.

How we measured

The board on daslang.io runs the llama-bench protocol, and llama-bench cannot measure speculative decoding. So we built a ruler for ourselves: modules/dasLLAMA/harness/mtp_ruler.das. It renders four chat prompts through the model's own template with thinking off, then runs two engines on the identical rendered text, greedy, exactly 128 tokens each, three repetitions, and writes one dated, sha-stamped JSON per box and model.

Ours runs as the release executable - the same artifact the board uses - on a sidecar minted the same day. The ruler starts it with the box's own settings:

DAS_TUNE_MANIFEST= DASLLAMA_MTP_HEAD="/Users/dasbox/models/mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q8_0.gguf" "modules/dasLLAMA/performance/_rig/dasllama-bench.app/Contents/MacOS/dasllama-bench" -- -m "/Users/dasbox/models/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf" --mtp-ab --mtp-depth 1 -n 128 -r 3 --ngl 99 --prompts "modules/dasLLAMA/benchmarks/data/specbench4_prompts.txt" --chat-prompts

llama.cpp runs as a stock llama-server built from upstream at commit 6fdd0ac89 - no fork, no patch - fed the same rendered prompt raw through /completion with ignore_eos, so it generates exactly 128 tokens too. The ruler starts it, per depth K, as llama-server --port P --host 127.0.0.1 -ngl 99 -fa on -c 2048 -t T -np 1 --no-warmup -fit off -m MODEL --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max K -md HEAD -ngld 99 (the function is run_lcpp_arm; T is the box's thread count, 10 on the M4 Pro) and reads the server's own timings back.

The prompts are the first turns of four Spec-Bench tasks (hemingkx/Spec-Bench, Apache-2.0): writing (qid 81), summarization (qid 241), GSM8K math (qid 401) and qa (qid 321), in modules/dasLLAMA/benchmarks/data/specbench4_prompts.txt. Both engines read the same drafter file: the Qwen NextN head as mtp-Qwen3.8-27B-Q8_0.gguf, the Gemma assistant as mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-Q8_0.gguf; the JSON records carry their sha256.

Two lessons the ruler now enforces, because each one cost us an afternoon:

  • Same thinking mode on both sides. Our first llama.cpp pass ran with thinking on and ours with thinking off, and their acceptance read 91%. A thinking-on continuation is an outline, not a blog post; it is a different text and a different acceptance rate. The ruler renders one prompt and hands it to both.
  • Settle before every arm. A heat-soaked Mac under-reads a memory-bound decode by 13 to 18%. Every arm waits 180 seconds on the dense 27B before it measures, the way the board driver does. And the release executable runs first: a parent process that had already run the engine in-process made the child's speculative arm read 20% low.

The invocation on the M4 Pro, verbatim:

bin/daslang -jit modules/dasLLAMA/harness/mtp_ruler.das -- -m $HOME/models/Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf --server $HOME/llama.cpp-ref-6fdd0ac/build-stock/bin/llama-server --depths 1,2 -t 10 --settle 180 -o modules/dasLLAMA/performance/records/mtp_m4_Qwen3.8-27B.json

What it measured

Tokens per second over 128 generated tokens, four prompts, three repetitions; acceptance in parentheses is accepted drafts over drafts offered. llama.cpp's pooled figure is the mean of its four prompt rows. Sources: the four mtp_*.json records named at the top of this story.

model, box (date, das sha) das off das depth 1 das depth 2 llama.cpp off n_max 1 n_max 2
gemma-4-26B-A4B Q4_K_M, M5 Max (09-02, ecf965ce5) 122.7 145.9 (75.2%) 148.1 (62.6%) 97.7 133.7 142.0
gemma-4-26B-A4B Q4_K_M, M4 Pro (09-02, e58e5a3ba) 59.2 67.5 (74.6%) 55.6 (62.9%) 52.8 67.2 62.5
Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M, M5 Max (09-02, 59cad510c) 27.6 33.0 (77.4%) 31.4 (75.1%) 25.2 34.1 33.5
Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M, M4 Pro (09-03, 24d13f1d2) 12.7 14.0 (77.4%) 12.4 (75.1%) 11.5 13.8 12.5

Per prompt, the two ends of the range. Gemma on the M5 Max:

prompt das off das depth 1 das depth 2 llama.cpp off n_max 1 n_max 2
writing 124.2 144.0 (69.3%) 138.3 (50.8%) 98.2 139.6 (81.4%) 130.8 (60.0%)
summarization 118.1 133.4 (69.3%) 124.6 (54.9%) 95.8 119.8 (70.3%) 126.0 (56.8%)
math 123.9 160.1 (89.6%) 187.9 (88.0%) 98.4 145.8 (89.6%) 163.4 (84.0%)
qa 124.8 148.6 (74.0%) 155.5 (63.4%) 98.2 129.5 (76.4%) 147.9 (70.5%)

Qwen 3.8 on the M4 Pro:

prompt das off das depth 1 das depth 2 llama.cpp off n_max 1 n_max 2
writing 12.8 13.5 (70.7%) 10.9 (59.3%) 11.5 13.6 (75.0%) 12.3 (66.7%)
summarization 12.6 14.0 (80.3%) 12.0 (71.7%) 11.5 13.8 (81.4%) 12.4 (69.8%)
math 12.8 15.4 (93.9%) 13.6 (86.2%) 11.5 14.5 (93.8%) 13.9 (87.0%)
qa 12.8 13.2 (67.1%) 13.8 (88.0%) 11.5 13.5 (80.0%) 11.5 (62.5%)

Acceptance is the same drafter on both sides and it shows: 75 to 94% at position 1 depending on the prompt, on both engines. The drafter is not where the two engines differ.

The arithmetic of a round

Here is the honest core. A depth-1 round produces on average 1 + a tokens, where a is the acceptance rate, so its speedup over plain decode is (1 + a) / c, with c the round's cost in plain steps. Read c back from the tables: c = (1 + a) / speedup.

model, box das round, in steps llama.cpp round, in steps
gemma, M5 Max 1.75 / 1.19 = 1.47 1.79 / 1.37 = 1.31
gemma, M4 Pro 1.75 / 1.14 = 1.53 1.83 / 1.27 = 1.44
Qwen 3.8, M5 Max 1.77 / 1.20 = 1.48 1.83 / 1.35 = 1.35
Qwen 3.8, M4 Pro 1.77 / 1.10 = 1.61 1.82 / 1.20 = 1.52

A round that verifies two rows costs both engines about one and a half plain steps, and that - not the drafter - is what caps the gain at 1.1 to 1.2x on a 27B dense model. The two extra rows' worth of work is the same weight pass read for two activation columns instead of one, plus the drafter, plus the bookkeeping. On the M4 Pro the round's own clocks on 2026-09-03 (build 24d13f1d2, plain step 78.7 ms) read: draft 7.4 ms, verify 119.0 ms, walk and commit 1.0 ms, replay 0.7 ms. Ninety-three percent of the round is the verify, and the verify is 1.51 plain steps for two rows.

That is also why depth 2 loses on the M4 Pro and only breaks even on the M5: a third row costs another 0.5 to 1.0 steps, and the second draft position is accepted 51 to 66% of the time, which does not cover it. Except on the math prompt, where position 2 runs 86 to 88% and depth 2 wins on every box (187.9 against 160.1 for gemma on the M5). Acceptance is the prompt's property. The box knob is the right default; the prompt-driven knob is the next idea.

Where the day went

The M4 Pro Qwen row is the one that moved. On the morning of 2026-09-02 it read 12.7 off and 11.0 at depth 1 - speculation was a loss on that box - while llama.cpp's read 11.5 and 13.6. The ruler said we were slow, and the ruler was the only reason we knew: on the M4's own terms, a 2.06-step round for two rows looked like the price of a small GPU.

The lab said otherwise. Our two-row kernel cost 1.36 to 1.49x of two single-row passes on the M4 Pro, and 0.52 to 0.89x on the M5 Max - the same kernel, two verdicts. A kernel shaped like llama.cpp's own sat at 0.9 to 1.05x on the M4. So we wrote the two-row register tile, raced it, crowned it on the M4 (0.48 ms against the old form's 0.84 on the race shape) and not on the M5 (0.53 against 0.49), and the row went to 13.9. Then the depth-2 row - 7.9 tok/s, 0.62x of plain - turned out to be the same story one row up: three rows took the four-column kernel, which no race had ever looked at. Walking the crowned tile over column pairs took the depth-2 row to 12.4 and the depth-1 row to 14.0 by the evening of 09-03. The whole fix is about a hundred lines and a test; finding it took a yardstick.

The yardstick

llama.cpp is the gold standard of local inference and it is the yardstick in every table here, not the opponent. Both projects are open source; they are welcome to anything in this engine with the license's attribution, and we take anything legal from anywhere. On this corpus, on these two boxes, on these two days: plain decode is ours by 10 to 26%, the speculative rounds land within a few percent of each other in both directions, and their depth-2 round is cheaper than ours. The ledger item for that last one is open.

Everything above reproduces from the commands shown, on the dates and shas shown. The records are in modules/dasLLAMA/performance/records/; the ruler renders any of them back into these tables with --render.

entry.title: Apple M5 support lands - text, vision and speech, tuned on the new silicon.
entry.content: dasLLAMA now treats the Apple M5 as a first-class target: the Metal 4 tensor units where the per-box race crowns them, the vision and speech encoders on the GPU, and the CPU lane on the M5 Max's all-compute core layout. The full M5 Max board is re-minted and on the board - gemma-4-E2B Q8_0 at 9074.3 / 161.3 tok/s (llama.cpp 7413.4 / 137.0), Qwen3.8-27B at 913.9 / 27.8 (752.1 / 25.4), pp512 / tg128 on Metal. Bringing a chip up one model at a time, and why it was fun: the story.

entry.title: Bringing up the Apple M5, one model at a time.
entry.content:
An M5 Max arrived at the end of August and became the main box the same day. dasLLAMA had never run on it. Everything below happened in the week that followed.

What a new chip is, to this engine

dasLLAMA does not ship kernels tuned for a chip. It ships kernel families - several ways to compute the same GEMV, attention or norm - and a tuner that races them on the box it is running on, then writes the winners into a sidecar. So "supporting the M5" is not a port. It is letting the races run and looking hard at every place where the winner changed.

Three things changed.

The GPU tensor units. The M5 GPU exposes tensor units through the Metal 4 tensor API. We wrote the tensor-side twin for each matrix family and let the race decide, per family, whether the tensor form or the simdgroup form wins on this box. On the M5 Max the tensor twins took every K-quant matmul family, the bf16 and q8 matmuls, the MoE matmuls and the attention QK matmul. The crown is a runtime knob in the sidecar, not a class default: a box that did not race keeps the simdgroup form, and a box that raced and lost keeps it too.

The CPU core layout. The M5 Max has no efficiency cores. It has 6 "Super" cores and 12 "Performance" cores, all compute. Our CPU lane had learned, on the M4, to exclude the efficiency tier from the pool; on the M5 that rule would have thrown away a third of the chip. The pool now spans both tiers, and decode parks the slower tier. Both core gates were verified live during the sweep, on both boxes.

The other modalities. The vision towers and the speech-to-text encoders serve on the GPU on the M5 the way the text path does. Nothing new in the design here - the same Metal rails - but each one had to be re-raced and its crowns re-minted.

What it measured

The full M5 Max board was re-minted on 2026-08-30 and is on the board (pp512 / tg128, Metal, llama-bench protocol), from modules/dasLLAMA/performance/records/m5.json:

model das pp512 / tg128 llama.cpp pp512 / tg128
gemma-4-E2B Q8_0 9074.3 / 161.3 7413.4 / 137.0
Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M 913.9 / 27.8 752.1 / 25.4
Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M 3752.9 / 165.7 3422.4 / 137.0
gpt-oss-20b mxfp4 3995.1 / 162.7 3476.6 / 149.0

The other modalities on the same box and day: the gemma-4-12B image encode 7.1 ms against the reference's 95 ms; the Qwen2.5-Omni window ViT 106 ms against 118; whisper large-v3-turbo transcribing jfk in 140 ms against whisper-cli's 153 on the same GPU.

The M4 board rows were refreshed alongside (m4.json, 2026-08-31), including Canary-Qwen on its new Q8_0 serving artifact: jfk in 307.6 ms on the M5 and 512.9 on the M4, beside the NeMo torch-MPS reference's 704.7 and 1076.5. On the long gb1 clip the das row reads 6484 ms beside the reference's 4383 - the one gap left on long audio, and the next dig. The M1 board stands unchanged as the long-term record; its Canary rows retire with the old decoder artifact.

Why it was fun

Because nothing about it was a port. Every kernel that had been tuned for one generation got raced again on the next, and the outcomes were not predictable from the spec sheet: some winners stayed, some flipped, and a few families needed a new form written before the race had anything worth crowning. Watching an engine re-tune itself to a chip that did not exist when the engine was written - and finding the handful of places where it could not, and fixing those - is the part of this project we would do for free.

entry.title: Qwen 3.8 27B joins the board - the new dense hybrid runs on CPU and Metal.
entry.content:
Qwen 3.8 27B is out, and it needed no new architecture support in dasLLAMA: the 3.8 generation keeps the qwen3.5 architecture - Gated-DeltaNet recurrent layers interleaved 3:1 with gated full attention - so it loads on the existing family path as a pure scale-up. The Q4_K_M file's attention and FFN planes serve natively on the kq rails, CPU and Metal alike (the DeltaNet projections transcode to q8 at load), and the model joins the official board catalog.

On an M1 Max (pp512 / tg128, llama-bench protocol): Metal - das 147.0 / 14.5 tok/s, llama.cpp 137.6 / 11.5; CPU - das 33.2 / 5.8, llama.cpp 29.8 / 5.6. On an M4 Pro: Metal - das 127.0 / 12.8, llama.cpp 126.2 / 11.5; CPU - das 45.8 / 11.6, llama.cpp 40.4 / 11.0. Full rows for both boxes are on the board.

entry.title: Metal support lands in speech-to-text - whisper large-v3-turbo at 49x realtime on an M1 Max.
entry.content: Speech-to-text now serves on Metal: whisper's cross-attention and decoder run on the GPU by default on Apple silicon, and the full-GPU mode powers the new gpu category on the board. On an M1 Max, whisper large-v3-turbo transcribes a 3:19 clip in 4.0 s - 49x realtime, against 36x for whisper.cpp's Metal path and 12x for our CPU lane. The board now splits ASR into the same cpu / cpu + accel / gpu categories the LLM board has.
